body:
Understanding Indian Space Missions

India's space programme includes missions to study the Moon, Mars and the Sun, observe distant astronomical objects, monitor Earth and demonstrate technologies needed for future space activities. The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) carries out these missions, sometimes in partnership with other space agencies.

For preliminary examinations, three questions are especially important: What was the mission intended to do? Which year was it launched? What did it actually achieve? A mission's launch, arrival at its destination and completion of its objective may occur in different years.

Basic Terms Needed to Understand the Missions

A natural satellite is a celestial body that revolves around another body, such as the Moon around Earth. An artificial satellite is a human-made spacecraft placed into orbit for observation, communication, scientific research or other purposes. Gravity helps keep an orbiting spacecraft moving around the body it orbits.

  • Orbiter: A spacecraft that travels around a celestial body and studies it remotely. An orbiter can examine a planet or moon without landing on its surface.
  • Lander: A spacecraft designed to descend onto a surface. A soft landing means reaching the surface in a controlled manner without a destructive impact.
  • Rover: A mobile robotic vehicle that moves across a surface and makes observations or measurements at different locations.
  • Space observatory: A spacecraft equipped to observe the Sun, stars or other astronomical sources using scientific instruments.
  • Earth observation satellite: A spacecraft that collects information about Earth's land, water, ice, vegetation or atmosphere.
  • Technology demonstration mission: A mission intended primarily to prove that a particular space operation or technology can work.

These descriptions identify the spacecraft's role, not necessarily its destination. For example, a spacecraft can orbit Earth, the Moon or Mars. A mission can also contain more than one component, such as an orbiter, lander and rover.

Indian Space Missions at a Glance

MissionLaunch yearPrincipal objective
Chandrayaan-12008Map and investigate the Moon's surface, minerals and chemical composition.
Chandrayaan-22019Study the Moon from orbit and attempt soft landing and rover exploration.
Chandrayaan-32023Demonstrate safe soft landing, rover movement and scientific experiments on the Moon.
Mangalyaan2013Orbit Mars and study its surface features and atmosphere.
Aditya-L12023Study the Sun, its outer atmosphere, solar activity and solar wind.
XPoSat2024Measure X-ray polarisation from astronomical sources.
SPADEX2024Demonstrate rendezvous, docking and undocking of spacecraft in orbit.
NISAR2025Use radar to monitor changes in Earth's land, ice, water and vegetation.

Why Launch Year and Achievement Year May Differ

A launch places a spacecraft on the initial part of its journey. The spacecraft may need additional time to reach its destination or complete an experiment. This distinction explains several important dates:

  • Mangalyaan was launched in 2013 but entered Mars orbit in 2014.
  • Aditya-L1 was launched in 2023 but entered its intended halo orbit around the Sun-Earth L1 point in 2024.
  • SPADEX was launched in 2024 but first achieved spacecraft docking in 2025.
  • NISAR was launched in 2025 and entered its science phase later that year.

Therefore, a question asking when a mission was launched is different from one asking when its principal achievement occurred.

The years in the table are launch years. Operational-status information in this lesson is based on official updates available through 4 November 2026. Launch dates are historical facts, whereas a spacecraft's operational status can change.

Prelims focus

  • Chandrayaan missions study the Moon; Mangalyaan studied Mars.
  • Aditya-L1 studies the Sun; XPoSat observes X-rays from astronomical sources.
  • SPADEX demonstrates spacecraft docking rather than studying a planet.
  • NISAR is an Earth observation mission jointly developed by NASA and ISRO.
  • Trap: Do not confuse a mission's launch year with its arrival, landing or docking year.

[NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 17, 'Stars and the Solar System', pp. 225-233, 2018-19 edition; NCERT, The Earth: Our Habitat, Class 6, Chapter 1, 'The Earth in the Solar System', pp. 1-5, 2018-19 edition; ISRO, 'Spacecraft Missions', mission list; ISRO, 'Mars Orbiter Mission', FAQ; ISRO, 'SpaDeX Mission', objectives; NASA, 'NISAR', mission overview. Online sources consulted 4 November 2026.]

body:
The Purpose of the Chandrayaan Programme

Chandrayaan refers to India's series of missions to explore the Moon. Lunar exploration helps scientists understand the Moon's surface, rocks, minerals, chemical composition and environment. Different observations can also provide evidence about the Moon's formation and geological history.

The first three Chandrayaan missions illustrate a progression from investigating the Moon from orbit to successfully operating robotic equipment on its surface. Their objectives and achievements must be distinguished carefully.

Chandrayaan-1: Studying the Moon from Orbit

Chandrayaan-1 was launched on 22 October 2008. It was India's first mission to the Moon. Its principal scientific objective was to map the lunar surface and investigate its chemical and mineral composition.

Its instruments studied the Moon using different types of radiation and imaging techniques. The mission produced information about lunar terrain, mineral distribution and geological features. It also carried a Moon Impact Probe, which was released toward the lunar surface.

One of Chandrayaan-1's most important scientific results was evidence of water molecules and hydroxyl on the lunar surface. This finding improved scientific understanding of the presence and distribution of water-related material on the Moon.

Evidence of water molecules or hydroxyl on the lunar surface does not mean that Chandrayaan-1 discovered lakes, rivers or oceans of liquid water on the Moon.

Chandrayaan-1 completed its major mission objectives before communication with the spacecraft was lost in August 2009. It was primarily a lunar-orbiting scientific mission, not a soft-landing mission.

Chandrayaan-2: Lunar Orbiter and Landing Attempt

Chandrayaan-2 was launched on 22 July 2019. It was designed to investigate the Moon through an orbiter and to demonstrate surface exploration using a lander and rover.

The mission consisted of three principal components:

  • Orbiter: Designed to study lunar topography, minerals, water-related material and other surface characteristics from orbit.
  • Vikram lander: Designed to perform a controlled soft landing on the Moon.
  • Pragyan rover: Intended to move across the lunar surface after deployment from the lander.

Chandrayaan-2 successfully entered lunar orbit in August 2019. However, during the landing attempt on 7 September 2019, communication with the Vikram lander was lost. The intended soft landing was not achieved.

The failure of the landing attempt did not mean that the entire mission failed. Its orbiter continued to conduct scientific observations and remained listed as operational by ISRO at the 4 November 2026 content cutoff.

Chandrayaan-3: Successful Soft Landing and Rover Exploration

Chandrayaan-3 was launched on 14 July 2023. It followed Chandrayaan-2 and concentrated on demonstrating the ability to land safely on the Moon and conduct scientific activities on the lunar surface.

The mission had three main objectives:

  1. Demonstrate a safe and soft landing on the lunar surface.
  2. Demonstrate rover movement on the Moon.
  3. Conduct scientific experiments at the lunar surface.

On 23 August 2023, Chandrayaan-3's Vikram lander successfully soft-landed in the Moon's southern high-latitude region. The Pragyan rover subsequently moved onto the surface and carried out observations.

The lander and rover investigated the local environment, including surface temperature, seismic activity and the chemical composition of nearby lunar material. Measurements made directly at the location being studied are called in-situ measurements.

Chandrayaan-3 demonstrated the required landing and rover technologies successfully. Its original surface operations were planned for approximately 1 lunar day, equivalent to about 14 Earth days.

Chandrayaan-3 landed in the southern high-latitude or south polar region of the Moon. This should not be confused with landing at the exact geographical South Pole. The mission was robotic; it did not carry astronauts or return lunar samples to Earth.

How the Three Missions Differ

Chandrayaan-1 concentrated on investigating the Moon from orbit. Chandrayaan-2 combined a successful lunar orbiter with an unsuccessful landing attempt. Chandrayaan-3 achieved the soft landing and rover operation that Chandrayaan-2 had attempted.

The distinction is important because a spacecraft reaching lunar orbit is not the same achievement as a spacecraft landing on the lunar surface.

Prelims focus

  • 2008: Chandrayaan-1, India's first lunar mission; investigated lunar minerals and water-related molecules.
  • 2019: Chandrayaan-2; successful orbiter but unsuccessful Vikram landing attempt.
  • 2023: Chandrayaan-3; successful soft landing on 23 August.
  • Chandrayaan-3's lander was named Vikram and its rover was named Pragyan.
  • Chandrayaan-3 demonstrated safe landing, rover movement and in-situ scientific experiments.
  • Trap: Chandrayaan-2 did not achieve a successful soft landing, but its orbiter was successful.

Online sources consulted 4 November 2026.]

body:
Mangalyaan: India's Mars Orbiter Mission

Mangalyaan, officially called the Mars Orbiter Mission (MOM), was India's first interplanetary mission. An interplanetary mission sends a spacecraft beyond Earth's immediate orbital environment toward another planet or another region of the Solar System.

Mangalyaan was launched on 5 November 2013 from Sriharikota. After travelling through interplanetary space, it successfully entered orbit around Mars on 24 September 2014.

India thereby became the first country to successfully place a spacecraft into Mars orbit on its first attempt.

Scientific Objectives

The mission was designed to investigate Mars while also demonstrating India's ability to operate a spacecraft on an interplanetary journey.

Its scientific investigations included:

  • Surface features: Observing the visible features and physical appearance of Mars.
  • Morphology: Studying the shapes and characteristics of surface features.
  • Mineralogy: Investigating the mineral characteristics of the Martian surface.
  • Atmosphere: Studying aspects of the gases and surrounding environment of Mars.

The mission carried instruments such as the Mars Colour Camera to observe Mars. It also included instruments for studying atmospheric constituents, including a methane sensor.

Mangalyaan was an orbiter, not a lander or rover. Its successful arrival meant that the spacecraft entered orbit around Mars; it did not descend onto the Martian surface.

Mission Duration and Status

The mission was designed for an operational life of approximately 6 months after entering Mars orbit. However, it continued operating for about 8 years. Following the loss of communication in 2022, ISRO declared the spacecraft non-recoverable and the mission at its end of life.

Mangalyaan: launch in 2013; arrival at Mars in 2014; mission ended in 2022. The launch year and Mars-orbit insertion year are different.

Aditya-L1: India's Solar Observatory

Aditya-L1 is India's first space-based observatory dedicated to studying the Sun. It was launched on 2 September 2023.

Unlike a lunar or planetary exploration mission, Aditya-L1 is designed to observe the Sun and collect scientific measurements that help explain solar activity.

What Does Aditya-L1 Study?

The Sun is a star that produces light, heat and energetic particles. Its outer atmosphere is called the corona. Changes in solar activity can influence the space environment around Earth.

Aditya-L1 investigates:

  • Solar corona: The Sun's outer atmosphere and its physical behaviour.
  • Solar flares: Sudden, intense releases of electromagnetic radiation associated with solar activity.
  • Coronal mass ejections: Large eruptions of magnetised plasma from the Sun's outer atmosphere.
  • Solar wind: The continuous flow of charged particles outward from the Sun.
  • Space weather: Conditions in space influenced by solar activity that may affect satellites, navigation and communication systems.

Studying these phenomena helps scientists understand how the Sun behaves and how its activity can influence technological systems near Earth.

Where Is Aditya-L1 Located?

Aditya-L1 operates in a halo orbit around the Sun-Earth Lagrange point 1 (L1). The L1 point lies approximately 1.5 million km from Earth in the direction of the Sun.

A Lagrange point is a location in a system of two large orbiting bodies where their combined gravitational effects and the orbital motion allow a smaller spacecraft to maintain a useful relative position with suitable orbital control. At Sun-Earth L1, a spacecraft can observe the Sun continuously without the regular eclipses that some Earth-orbiting spacecraft experience.

Aditya-L1 does not sit motionless at L1. It follows a halo orbit around that point and requires occasional corrections to maintain its intended path.

Aditya-L1 entered its intended halo orbit on 6 January 2024. It carries scientific instruments to observe the Sun and measure particles and magnetic fields near the spacecraft.

The mission remained active at the 4 November 2026 cutoff. An ISRO update dated 3 November 2026 reported scientific results obtained using Aditya-L1 observations.

Aditya-L1 does not land on or orbit close to the surface of the Sun. Its observation location is approximately 1.5 million km from Earth toward the Sun, not 1.5 million km from the Sun itself.

Distinguishing Mangalyaan from Aditya-L1

Both missions involved spacecraft travelling beyond ordinary Earth observation orbits, but their destinations and purposes differ fundamentally. Mangalyaan entered orbit around Mars to study a planet. Aditya-L1 operates near the Sun-Earth L1 point to observe the Sun and investigate solar activity.

Mangalyaan's launch and Mars arrival occurred in different years. The same is true of Aditya-L1's launch and halo-orbit insertion.

Prelims focus

  • Mangalyaan: Launched on 5 November 2013; entered Mars orbit on 24 September 2014.
  • Mangalyaan studied the Martian surface, minerals and atmosphere; it did not land on Mars.
  • Mangalyaan's mission ended in 2022 after approximately 8 years in Mars orbit.
  • Aditya-L1: Launched on 2 September 2023; entered its halo orbit on 6 January 2024.
  • Aditya-L1 studies the Sun from around the Sun-Earth L1 point, approximately 1.5 million km from Earth.
  • Trap: Aditya-L1 is a solar observatory, not a mission that landed on the Sun.

[NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 17, 'Stars and the Solar System', pp. 225-229, 2018-19 edition; NCERT, The Earth: Our Habitat, Class 6, Chapter 1, 'The Earth in the Solar System', pp. 1-4, 2018-19 edition; ISRO, 'FAQ - Mars Orbiter Mission', questions 1-6; ISRO, 'Update on the Mars Orbiter Mission', 3 October 2022; ISRO, 'Aditya-L1', mission science objectives; ISRO, 'Aditya-L1 Mission: Completion of First Halo Orbit', 2 July 2024; ISRO, 'India's Aditya-L1 Reveals the Hidden Third Dimension of a Solar Eruption', 3 November 2026. Online sources consulted 4 November 2026.]
